questions.stem: A 6-year-old child had a tonsillectomy this morning. At 1600 the nurse notes the child is swallowing every few seconds and has vomited a small amount of bright red blood. The child is restless and pale. Heart rate has risen from 98 to 136/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the child is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

condition.text: Expected swallowing of old blood after surgery

actions.text: Position the child on the side with the head slightly down
Have the child gargle with cold water to slow the bleeding
Suction deep into the back of the throat to see where the blood is coming from
Give a dose of ibuprofen for pain and recheck in an hour

parameters.text: Frequency of swallowing and amount of blood
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants
Urine specific gravity with each void

rationale.correct: After tonsillectomy, frequent swallowing, bright red blood and tachycardia signal hemorrhage; position on the side, notify the surgeon and watch swallowing and vital signs.

perOption.c1: Frequent swallowing, bright red vomit, restlessness and tachycardia after tonsillectomy point to bleeding from the surgical site.
perOption.c2: Old blood is dark brown; bright red blood with tachycardia is active bleeding.
perOption.c3: Nausea does not explain frequent swallowing and rising heart rate.
perOption.c4: Dehydration does not cause bright red vomit.
perOption.a1: Active bleeding may need a return to the operating room.
perOption.a2: Side-lying lets blood drain from the mouth and protects the airway.
perOption.a3: Gargling can dislodge clots and worsen bleeding.
perOption.a4: Deep suction can injure the surgical site.
perOption.a5: NSAIDs can increase bleeding, and waiting is unsafe.
perOption.p2: Rising heart rate is an early sign of blood loss in children; hypotension is late.
perOption.p5: Not a guide to acute bleeding.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: The nurse has just drawn an arterial blood gas sample from a client's radial artery. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the site for at least 5 minutes
Shake the syringe hard to mix the blood with the heparin
Leave an air bubble in the syringe so the sample keeps its oxygen level
Send the sample at room temperature at the end of the shift with other specimens

rationale.correct: After an ABG: hold firm pressure for at least 5 minutes, remove air bubbles, label and send promptly.

perOption.a: Arterial punctures bleed more than venous ones; pressure for 5 minutes or longer (longer with anticoagulants) prevents a hematoma.
perOption.b: Vigorous shaking can damage cells; the sample is rolled gently.
perOption.c: Air bubbles change the oxygen and carbon dioxide values and must be removed.
perOption.d: Gas samples must be analyzed promptly, usually within minutes, or on ice per policy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: Four hours after a colonoscopy with removal of several polyps, a client reports severe abdominal pain that is getting worse. The abdomen is rigid and tender, temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) and heart rate is 118/min. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Gas pain from the air used to inflate the colon during the procedure
Perforation of the bowel wall with leakage of contents
A reaction to the bowel preparation solution taken the night before
Expected discomfort from the sedation as it wears off over the evening

rationale.correct: After colonoscopy, severe or worsening abdominal pain, rigidity, fever or tachycardia suggest perforation and need urgent reporting.

perOption.a: Mild cramping from air is common, but it eases and does not cause rigidity and fever.
perOption.b: Severe, worsening pain, a rigid abdomen, fever and tachycardia after polyp removal suggest perforation and peritonitis.
perOption.c: Bowel prep effects occur before the procedure and do not cause peritonitis.
perOption.d: Sedation does not cause abdominal rigidity or fever.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes has a hemoglobin A1C of 9.1%. The client says their morning fingerstick readings have been "pretty good." How should the nurse interpret the A1C?

options.text: It shows glucose has been well controlled, since the morning readings are good
It shows average glucose over about 3 months has been well above the usual target
It reflects just the glucose level on the day the blood sample was drawn at the lab
It is a test of kidney function that is affected by diabetes over time

rationale.correct: A1C reflects average glucose over 2 to 3 months; most adults with diabetes aim for under 7%. Good morning readings can hide high levels later in the day.

perOption.a: An A1C of 9.1% shows high average glucose regardless of the morning readings.
perOption.b: A1C reflects average glucose over 2 to 3 months; 9.1% is well above the usual goal of under 7%.
perOption.c: A1C reflects the past 2 to 3 months, not one day.
perOption.d: A1C measures glucose attached to hemoglobin, not kidney function.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a CT scan of the abdomen with IV contrast this afternoon. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider before the scan?

options.text: The client had an allergic reaction to shrimp as a child
A serum creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL, up from 1.1 last month
The client ate a light breakfast at 0700 this morning
The client is anxious and asks how long the scan will take

rationale.correct: Before IV contrast, check kidney function, earlier contrast reactions and metformin use; shellfish allergy is not a contraindication.

perOption.a: Shellfish allergy does not predict a reaction to iodinated contrast.
perOption.b: Worsening kidney function raises the risk of contrast-associated kidney injury; the provider may change the plan or give fluids.
perOption.c: Fasting rules vary, and a light early meal is often acceptable; it is less important than kidney function.
perOption.d: Anxiety is addressed with explanation; it does not change safety.

questions.stem: A client who had a thoracotomy 2 days ago has an epidural catheter for pain control and receives enoxaparin for clot prevention. The client now reports new back pain and cannot lift either leg off the bed. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Expected motor block from the epidural medication
An epidural hematoma that is pressing on the spinal cord
Muscle stiffness from lying in bed for 2 days after surgery
A urinary tract infection spreading to the kidneys

rationale.correct: With an epidural catheter and anticoagulation, new back pain or leg weakness or numbness suggests epidural hematoma; notify the provider urgently, as decompression may be needed.

perOption.a: Low-dose epidural analgesia usually spares motor function; new weakness with back pain is a warning sign.
perOption.b: Back pain with new leg weakness in a client with an epidural and an anticoagulant suggests a hematoma, a surgical emergency.
perOption.c: Stiffness does not cause inability to lift the legs.
perOption.d: Kidney infection causes flank pain and fever, not leg weakness.

questions.stem: A client is on the first day after an open bowel resection. Which interventions help prevent postoperative complications? Select all that apply.

options.text: Walking in the hall at least three times today
Using the incentive spirometer 10 times an hour while awake
Keeping the legs crossed in bed for comfort
Wearing sequential compression devices while in bed
Splinting the incision with a pillow when coughing
Staying in bed until the incision is fully healed

rationale.correct: Postoperative prevention: early walking, incentive spirometry, compression devices, splinted coughing and avoiding leg crossing and prolonged bed rest.

perOption.a: Early walking prevents clots, pneumonia and ileus.
perOption.c: Crossing the legs slows venous return and raises clot risk.
perOption.d: Compression devices reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis.
perOption.e: Splinting reduces pain and lets the client cough effectively.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client reports fatigue, weight gain, constipation and feeling cold. Laboratory results show a TSH of 18 mU/L (high) and a free T4 of 0.4 ng/dL (low). How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: They suggest primary hypothyroidism from an underactive thyroid
They suggest hyperthyroidism from Graves' disease
They suggest a pituitary tumor causing too much growth hormone
They are normal results for an older adult and need no follow-up

rationale.correct: Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH and low free T4, with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation.

perOption.a: A high TSH with a low T4 shows the thyroid is underactive and the pituitary is trying to stimulate it.
perOption.b: Graves' disease causes low TSH and high T4.
perOption.c: Growth hormone excess does not cause this pattern.

questions.stem: A client with untreated Graves' disease is admitted with pneumonia. Today the client is agitated and confused, with a temperature of 40.2 °C (104.4 °F), heart rate 168/min in atrial fibrillation, blood pressure 164/62 mm Hg, vomiting and diarrhea. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Give the prescribed beta-blocker such as propranolol
Give the prescribed antithyroid drug, followed later by iodine as ordered
Give aspirin by mouth or rectally to bring down the high fever
Wrap the client in warm blankets to stop the shivering and chills
Give the client's prescribed levothyroxine dose as soon as possible

parameters.text: Body weight measured once a week
Visual acuity with an eye chart each day
Serum albumin and total protein levels

rationale.correct: Thyroid storm: beta-blocker, antithyroid drug then iodine, steroids, cooling with acetaminophen (not aspirin) and close cardiac and temperature monitoring.

perOption.c1: High fever, rapid atrial fibrillation, agitation and GI symptoms in untreated Graves' disease triggered by infection are thyroid storm.
perOption.c2: Sepsis causes fever, but a widened pulse pressure, rapid AF and agitation with Graves' disease point to thyroid storm.
perOption.c3: Myxedema coma causes low temperature and slow heart rate.
perOption.c4: There is no history of heat exposure.
perOption.a1: Beta-blockers control heart rate and adrenergic symptoms.
perOption.a2: Antithyroid drugs block hormone production; iodine is given after to block release.
perOption.a3: Aspirin can raise free thyroid hormone levels; acetaminophen is used instead.
perOption.a5: Thyroid hormone would worsen the crisis.
perOption.p1: Rapid AF and heart failure are major dangers.
perOption.p2: Shows whether cooling and treatment are working.
perOption.p3: Not useful in an acute crisis.
perOption.p4: Not a key parameter in thyroid storm.
perOption.p5: Not a guide to thyroid storm.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client on home peritoneal dialysis calls the clinic and says the fluid draining out this morning looks cloudy. The client also has mild abdominal pain and feels warm. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: A normal change in the dialysate after a large meal
Peritonitis, an infection of the lining of the abdomen
Too much fluid being removed during each exchange
A blocked catheter that needs to be flushed at home

rationale.correct: Cloudy peritoneal dialysis effluent is peritonitis until proven otherwise; the client needs a sample sent and antibiotics, often added to the dialysate.

perOption.a: Cloudy effluent is not a normal finding.
perOption.b: Cloudy effluent with abdominal pain and fever is the classic sign of peritonitis, the main complication of peritoneal dialysis.
perOption.c: Excess removal causes dehydration and low blood pressure, not cloudy fluid.
perOption.d: A blocked catheter slows drainage but does not make it cloudy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with a severe asthma attack has been wheezing loudly for an hour despite albuterol treatments. The client is now quieter, very drowsy, and the nurse hears almost no wheezing or air movement. SpO2 is 86%. What does this change most likely mean?

options.text: The bronchodilator has worked and the attack is ending
The client is tiring and air movement is too poor to produce wheezing
The client has developed a pneumothorax on one side
The client is falling asleep because the anxiety of the attack has finally resolved

rationale.correct: In severe asthma, decreasing wheezing with drowsiness and poor air movement is a silent chest, an emergency signaling respiratory failure.

perOption.a: Improvement would bring better air movement and alertness, not drowsiness and low oxygen.
perOption.b: A "silent chest" with drowsiness signals impending respiratory failure; the client may need intubation.
perOption.c: Pneumothorax causes absent sounds on one side, but this picture fits exhaustion and severe obstruction.
perOption.d: Drowsiness with low oxygen is a danger sign, not relief.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes is prescribed insulin lispro before meals. The breakfast tray arrives at 0800. When should the nurse give the lispro?

options.text: Within 15 minutes before the client starts to eat the meal
One hour before breakfast so the insulin is at its peak when the tray arrives
At bedtime, so it covers the glucose rise overnight
Two hours after breakfast, once the blood glucose has risen

rationale.correct: Rapid-acting insulins (lispro, aspart, glulisine) are given within 15 minutes before a meal; the tray should be present.

perOption.a: Rapid-acting insulin starts working within about 15 minutes, so it is given just before eating.
perOption.b: Giving it an hour early can cause hypoglycemia before the meal.
perOption.c: Lispro is a mealtime insulin, not an overnight insulin.
perOption.d: Giving it late leaves the meal uncovered and then risks hypoglycemia.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client has a prescription for a new transdermal nitroglycerin patch each morning. Which action is correct?

options.text: Remove the old patch and use a different hairless site
Place the new patch on top of the old one so the dose stays steady
Cut the patch in half if the client gets a headache
Apply the new patch to the same spot each day so it sticks better

rationale.correct: Transdermal patches: remove the old patch, apply to clean, hairless, rotated sites, do not cut and dispose of safely.

perOption.a: Removing the old patch prevents overdose, and rotating sites prevents skin irritation.
perOption.c: Patches should not be cut unless the product allows it.
perOption.d: Using the same site irritates the skin.

segments.text: The client is wearing compression stockings

perOption.s2: Cloudy, foul drainage suggests a leak of bowel contents and infection.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of sepsis after bowel surgery.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client is most likely experiencing {{b1}} caused by {{b2}}.

options.text: septic shock
hypovolemic shock from bleeding
cardiogenic shock
leakage at the bowel anastomosis
a urinary tract infection
a reaction to the anesthetic

rationale.correct: An anastomotic leak typically appears 3 to 7 days after bowel surgery with pain, fever, ileus and signs of sepsis.

perOption.b1:a: Infection with hypotension and a lactate above 4 mmol/L fits septic shock.
perOption.b1:b: The drain fluid is cloudy and foul, not bloody, and there is fever.
perOption.b2:a: Day 4 pain, distention and foul drain fluid after colectomy suggest anastomotic leak.
perOption.b2:b: The drain and abdominal findings point to the bowel.
perOption.b2:c: Anesthetic effects do not appear on day 4 with fever and foul drainage.

questions.stem: For each potential problem, indicate whether the client is at high or low immediate risk based on the current data.

rows.text: Wound dehiscence of the skin incision

rationale.correct: Septic shock threatens the kidneys, lungs and circulation; the intact incision is a lower immediate concern.

perOption.r1:c1: Urine output 15 mL/hr and creatinine doubled show the kidneys are affected.
perOption.r2:c1: Hypotension and a high lactate show shock is progressing.
perOption.r4:c1: Tachypnea from sepsis and abdominal distention can lead to respiratory failure.
perOption.r4:c2: The rising respiratory rate shows high risk.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse anticipate within the first hour? Select all that apply.

options.text: Draw blood cultures before giving antibiotics
Give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics as prescribed
Give a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus as prescribed
Prepare the client for possible return to surgery
Start a regular diet to improve the client's strength
Hold all IV fluids to avoid fluid overload
Repeat the lactate level after the fluid bolus

rationale.correct: Sepsis bundle: cultures, antibiotics, fluids, lactate and source control, such as surgery for an anastomotic leak.

perOption.d: A leak often needs surgical source control.
perOption.e: The client needs to be NPO with an ileus and possible surgery.
perOption.f: The client is in shock and needs fluids.
perOption.g: A falling lactate shows perfusion is improving.

questions.stem: After 2 L of crystalloid, the client's mean arterial pressure is 58 mm Hg, and norepinephrine is prescribed. The client has a peripheral IV in the forearm and a central line is being placed. While the infusion runs peripherally, the nurse sees the skin around the IV is cool, pale and swollen. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the rate of the norepinephrine to raise the pressure faster
Stop the infusion at that site and follow the extravasation protocol
Apply a warm compress and keep the infusion running at the same rate
Elevate the arm and recheck the site again in 1 hour

rationale.correct: Vasopressors are given through a central line when possible; with peripheral extravasation, stop the infusion at that site and use the protocol, which may include phentolamine.

perOption.a: Extravasation needs the infusion stopped at that site, not increased.
perOption.b: Norepinephrine extravasation can cause tissue necrosis; the infusion is moved and an antidote such as phentolamine may be given.
perOption.c: The infusion must be stopped in that vein.
perOption.d: Waiting allows tissue damage to continue.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client's low blood pressure is caused by {{b1}}, which happens because {{b2}}.

options.text: reduced venous return to the heart
bleeding into the abdomen
a heart attack caused by the crash
air is trapped and building pressure in the right chest
the left lung has collapsed
the client is hyperventilating from anxiety

rationale.correct: Tension pneumothorax traps air under pressure, collapsing the lung and pushing the mediastinum, which blocks venous return and causes shock.

perOption.b1:a: Pressure in the chest compresses the great veins and heart.
perOption.b1:b: The chest findings explain the low blood pressure.
perOption.b1:c: Nothing suggests MI; the mechanism is obstruction.
perOption.b2:a: A one-way leak lets air in but not out, shifting the mediastinum.
perOption.b2:c: Anxiety does not cause tracheal shift and hypotension.

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze the mechanism of tension pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should anticipate, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Prepare for chest tube insertion after decompression
Wait for a chest x-ray to confirm before any treatment
Lay the client flat with the legs raised
Give a sedative to calm the client's anxiety

parameters.text: Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants
Color and clarity of the urine

rationale.correct: Tension pneumothorax is treated by immediate needle decompression, then a chest tube, with close monitoring of oxygenation and blood pressure.

perOption.c1: Absent breath sounds, tracheal shift, distended neck veins and hypotension after chest trauma indicate tension pneumothorax.
perOption.c2: A simple pneumothorax does not cause tracheal shift and shock.
perOption.c3: Tamponade causes muffled heart sounds without tracheal shift or absent breath sounds on one side.
perOption.c4: Flail chest causes paradoxical chest movement, not tracheal shift.
perOption.a1: Needle decompression releases the trapped air and restores circulation.
perOption.a2: A chest tube provides definitive drainage.
perOption.a3: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; waiting is dangerous.
perOption.a5: Sedation can worsen breathing and does not treat the cause.
perOption.p2: Show whether circulation recovers after decompression.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A chest tube is inserted on the right and connected to a drainage system with suction. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the drainage system below the level of the chest
Check that the water seal chamber has water at the correct level
Clamp the tube routinely each time the client is turned
Keep sterile petroleum gauze and tape at the bedside
Tape all connections securely
Strip the tubing every hour to keep it open

rationale.correct: Chest tube care: system below the chest, water seal at the right level, secure connections, emergency supplies at the bedside and no routine clamping or stripping.

perOption.a: This prevents backflow into the pleural space.
perOption.b: The water seal prevents air from returning to the chest.
perOption.c: Routine clamping can cause a tension pneumothorax.
perOption.d: Needed if the tube is accidentally pulled out.
perOption.f: Stripping creates high negative pressure and is not recommended.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Manage a chest tube drainage system.

questions.stem: Two hours after the chest tube is placed, the nurse notes continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber that was not there before. The client's breathing is unchanged. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the suction to clear the extra air faster
Check the tubing and connections from the dressing down to find an air leak
Clamp the chest tube near the client for an hour to stop the bubbling
Remove the chest tube, since the bubbling shows that the lung has now fully re-expanded

rationale.correct: Continuous bubbling in the water seal means an air leak; check the system for loose connections, then report if it persists, since it may come from the lung.

perOption.a: Changing suction does not find the source of a new leak.
perOption.b: New continuous bubbling often means a leak in the system; checking from the client to the drainage unit finds it.
perOption.c: Prolonged clamping can cause a tension pneumothorax.
perOption.d: Bubbling does not mean the lung has re-expanded, and nurses do not remove chest tubes without orders.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

caseStudies.title: Tension pneumothorax after a car crash

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 2140
exhibits.body: A 32-year-old client was the driver in a car crash and hit the steering wheel. The client has right-sided chest pain, bruising across the chest and is becoming more anxious and short of breath. Breath sounds are absent on the right. The trachea is shifted to the left, and the neck veins are distended.
